inventory.name: Traveler's Pack
inventory.description: A worn canvas pack with good straps — bedroll, flint, mess kit, fifty small comforts of the road.

inventory.name: Waterskin
inventory.description: Boiled and refilled at the last clean spring. Worth more every week the river runs gray.

inventory.name: Medic's Satchel
inventory.description: Herb rolls, boiled linen, needle and gut. Valley medicine — patient, practical, proven.

inventory.name: Healing Draught
inventory.description: Bitter green tincture from the terrace gardens. Knits small wounds and dulls big ones.

inventory.name: Silver-Stemmed Cutting (linen-wrapped)
inventory.description: A two-node cutting from the uncatalogued east-terrace plants, wrapped in boiled linen. Root angle (20° below horizontal, south-southeast) and node spacing noted in charcoal on the margin. Pale sap at the cut end — no name for it yet.

chronicle: Adelheid wakes rested at Mara Wells' Store and eats before the dawn conversation; Mara refuses again to explain the map's full meaning or the Precursor system's destination, naming only that this question is what keeps her awake.

turns.player: Accept that Mara has her reasons and her method. Ask her what you SHOULD do right now—what does she need from you, here, today?
turns.summary: At Mara Wells' Store in early morning, Adelheid learns her task: walk the river west to track how far the contamination has spread, then find Edvar Crane at the mill to learn what he has read in the water these past three weeks. Mara refuses direct explanation but is clear that time is short and that Adelheid's observations—and her choice—will be crucial to what comes next.
turns.narration:
You set down your cup and meet Mara's eyes across the table. The store around you is still quiet—the light coming through the front windows is pale and thin, that particular spring gray that says the sun is still thinking about rising.

"You're not going to tell me where that system is headed," you say. It's not a question. "And you're not going to tell me why it matters that it's waking hours instead of weeks."

Mara doesn't look away. She nods, once.

"Then tell me what I should do right now. What does today need from me?"

She sets her own cup down with deliberate care. Her hands are steady, but there's something held in the line of her shoulders—not fear, but readiness. The kind of readiness that comes from making decisions in the dark and committing to them.

"Three things," Mara says. "First: do not go back to the terraces alone. Not today. Not until you understand what you're walking into."

Aevi dims slightly at your shoulder, her motes clustering tighter. She hums a low, questioning note.

"Second: the river is worse. You felt it yourself—the water moves wrong, reads wrong. I need you to walk the bank west from here, past where the gray-green breaks into ordinary green. I need to know how far the contamination has spread since yesterday. You can see things others miss. You'll notice what I cannot."

She leans forward slightly, and now her voice drops.

"Third, and this is the one that matters: Edvar Crane is at the mill. He's been reading the water for three weeks now—before the council knew to worry about it, before the Harmonic and Radiant started their public argument. He knows something. And he'll talk to you in a way he won't talk to me. Go to him after the river walk. Ask him what he's seen."

Mara pauses, and you feel the weight of what she's not saying yet.

"And Adelheid—when you've done those two things, come back here. There's a choice you'll need to make, and you'll understand it better once you've seen the water and heard what Edvar knows. But it needs to be your choice, not mine. That's how this works."

turns.player: Go to the mill first, before the river walk. Edvar might be more willing to talk early, before the day's work demands his attention—and what he tells you might guide what to look for on the bank.
turns.summary: At Mara Wells' Store, you choose to visit Edvar Crane at the mill first, reading the water-signs before the river walk. Mara confirms the plan with quiet approval and gives you written direction.
turns.narration:
You nod slowly, thinking it through. The river walk can wait—you need to know what Edvar has seen before you step out into the field to look for yourself. He'll be more himself now, before the mill's work swallows the morning, and what he's read in the water these past three weeks might be the thing that shapes what you're actually hunting for on the western bank.

Mara watches you work it out, and something in her expression settles—approval, quiet and operational. She reaches across the table and slides a small folded paper toward you. "His name and the mill's location, written plain. He knows you're coming. He's been waiting for someone to ask." Her voice carries no inflection, but the precision of it—*he's been waiting*—lands like confirmation that this errand has been threading through more than just her ledgers.

You tuck the paper into your satchel and stand. The store around you is beginning to stir—the pale morning light strengthening by degrees, a customer's footstep on the wooden walk outside. Aevi's motes brighten slightly at your shoulder, sensing the shift toward motion. The river work and whatever Edvar has learned are still ahead; but the day's weight is settling on your shoulders now, and you feel the shape of it—small choices making lines that might matter.

turns.player: Head to the mill now, moving fast through the early-morning streets.
turns.summary: Adelheid arrives at the mill in early morning to meet Edvar Crane, who has been waiting with three weeks of water-reading behind him.
turns.narration:
You step out of Mara's store into the early-spring morning, the folded paper tucked safe in your pocket. The streets of Millbrook are just beginning to stir—a woman sweeping her doorstep, a man loading a cart with clay pots, the smell of woodsmoke and something baking carried on air still cold enough to see your breath.

The mill lies on the river's south curve, and you know the way. Your feet find the pace without thinking—not quite running, but steady and fast, the kind of movement that doesn't draw eyes. The muddy paths between the terraces are slick from yesterday's melt, but your boots grip well enough. Behind you, Aevi's motes drift in loose formation, barely visible in the growing light.

You reach the mill in less than a quarter-hour. It's already awake—the great wheel creaks slowly at the waterline, not quite at full turn yet, and you can hear the work beginning inside: the grinding sound of the stones, a voice calling something unheard. A tall man stands at the mill's side entrance, arms crossed, watching the river.

He looks up as you approach. He has the particular stillness of someone who has spent weeks watching water and listening to it, the way it speaks when you know how to hear. His eyes are pale gray, river-colored, and very sharp.

turns.player: Step closer and offer your hand in greeting. Let him see you as Mara's messenger.
turns.summary: At the mill's south entrance, Edvar Crane refuses to meet your greeting as an ally. He is exhausted, distant, and speaks of the river's contamination as an active, waking thing. The water will not speak to you now.
turns.narration:
You cross the last stretch of mud-slick ground toward the mill's south entrance, your boots finding purchase on the wet earth. Edvar is still there, arms crossed, watching the river's gray-green surface with the particular stillness of someone who has learned to listen to water. He doesn't turn as you approach—he's heard you coming, your footsteps carrying through the damp air—but something in his shoulders tightens.

You raise your hand in greeting, stepping into his line of sight with an open palm, the gesture clear: you are Mara's messenger, and you come in peace. "Edvar," you say, keeping your voice level and warm. "Mara sent me. She said you've been waiting."

For a long moment, he doesn't move. His river-pale eyes slide toward you—not hostile, but distant, as though he's looking at something you cannot see standing behind where you are. When he finally speaks, his voice is thin and careful, the voice of someone rationing words like water in a drought.

"She sent you," he repeats. Not a question. Not quite agreement either. His gaze drifts back to the river. "But you're not listening yet. You came too fast. Too loud. The water won't speak to you now—you've brought the day with you, and it's not ready to be heard."

He uncrosses his arms and turns fully to face you, and for the first time you see the toll three weeks of watching has taken. His face is lined with exhaustion; there are stains on his sleeves that might be river-mud or might be something else. His eyes are the eyes of a man who has been drowning in small increments and has forgotten what breathing feels like.

"Mara wants me to tell you things," he says quietly. "But you have to understand first that the water is already gone. Three weeks ago it was gray-green at the edges. Now it's all the way through. And something beneath it is still waking."

turns.player: Step back and offer him time and quiet instead of greeting—sit by the wheel and wait for him to come to you.
turns.summary: At the mill, Edvar refuses your attempt at gentleness and demands direct engagement. His exhaustion is real and his patience is gone.
turns.narration:
You see the moment he's about to turn, and you read it wrong—the tension in his shoulders isn't readiness, it's exhaustion stretched past its limit. Instead of stepping closer with your hand out, you step back. You cross to the great mill wheel, its timber creaking as it turns on the current, and you sit down on a low stone bench worn smooth by seasons of use. The mud is cold through your coat, but you settle into it anyway. You wait.

Edvar's jaw tightens. He doesn't come to you. Instead, he turns fully to face you from where he stands, and when he speaks, his voice is thin and sharp as a blade of glass. "Mara sent you to wait for me to be ready to talk. That's not how this works." He gestures at the river with one tired hand—the water churns gray-green past the mill sills, thick with something that makes the light sit wrong on its surface. "The river doesn't wait. It doesn't get softer or easier to read if you sit quiet. It gets worse." He pauses, and you see the price of three weeks written in the hollow of his face. "You're here to listen or you're not. But silence won't open me up. I stopped being the kind of person silence helps about the time the water started dying."

turns.summary: At the mill, Edvar's guard drops slightly when asked about Silas Weir—his answer suggests a connection to the water crisis he has been tracking for three weeks.
turns.narration:
You turn back toward Edvar, your voice steady and deliberate. "Do you know Silas Weir?"

Edvar's sharp expression doesn't soften, but something shifts behind his eyes—a recognition, a weight settling deeper. He's quiet for a long moment, the mill wheel creaking its slow rhythm at the waterline. When he speaks, his voice carries less glass and more exhaustion underneath it.

"Silas. Yes." He turns back to the river, his shoulders dropping slightly. "He was at the Heights before—before the readings got bad. He's... connected to this. To what's happening." Edvar doesn't elaborate, but you hear the admission underneath: he knows something about Silas, and it matters to what he's been reading in the water. "Why are you asking me about him?"

Behind you, Aevi's motes brighten slightly—a quiet hum, almost inaudible, that suggests she heard something in his answer worth noting. The question hangs between you now, no longer about whether Edvar will talk, but about what he knows and why he's held it close.

turns.player: Ask if there is a garden that needs tending or work to be done
turns.summary: Returning to Mara Wells' Store after speaking with Edvar, Adelheid offers to work—and Mara directs her to the store's garden beds, where spring plants are breaking through the earth.
turns.narration:
You turn from the river and the weight of Edvar's admission, needing to move—to do something with your hands that isn't waiting or pushing. You make your way back through the mill's south entrance and onto the market lane, your boots finding the familiar path toward Mara Wells' Store.

The morning light is sharper now, the mist burned off. When you push open the store's door, the smell of dried herbs and sorted inventory meets you—orderly, purposeful. Mara is behind her counter, ledger open before her, but she looks up the moment you enter. She reads you quickly: mud on your knees, river-damp on your shoulders, the particular exhaustion of someone who has tried to move stone with words.

"Edvar wouldn't soften," she says. It isn't a question. "But he spoke." You nod. She closes the ledger with a deliberate motion and sets her pen aside. "There are always things that need hands here," she says, gesturing toward the back room where you can see shelves of harvest-work in progress—bundles needing sorting, jars waiting for labels, the endless maintenance of a store that keeps a village fed. "But more immediately: there's the garden. Spring plants are pushing through, and the beds need turning before the real heat comes. If your hands want work, they'll find it there."

turns.player: Begin turning the garden beds, working steadily while Mara moves nearby—let conversation arise naturally as your hands work
turns.summary: In Mara Wells' garden, turning spring beds side by side, Mara shifts the conversation toward a choice she's been holding back.
turns.narration:
You push through to the back room where the garden beds wait. The soil is still cold from the melt, but it's breaking up under the spade—clay and dark mulch turning over to meet the spring air. Your shoulders find the rhythm: push, turn, settle. Push, turn, settle. The work is simple and it steadies you.

Mara appears in the garden doorway without fanfare, carrying two cups of hot water and something green steeped in it. She sets one cup on the low bench where you can reach it, and she doesn't ask permission—she simply begins to turn the bed beside yours, her movements economical and practiced. For a few minutes there is only the sound of spades meeting earth and the drip of water from the eaves.

Then Mara speaks, her voice as unhurried as the work. "Edvar holds things close because he's been alone with them for three weeks. That's not the same as holding them from you." She turns another spadeful, doesn't look at you. "He admitted Silas was at the Heights. That's further than he's gone with anyone else. What he won't say yet is why it matters—but he will, when he's ready. Pushing won't open that door."

You feel Aevi's motes brighten slightly near your shoulder, attentive to the shift in Mara's tone. The older woman continues: "There's a second part to what I need from you. Not the river walk—that can wait. First, I need to know if you're truly willing to move into difficult ground. Because what comes next has a cost I haven't named yet."

turns.player: Ask what Silas Weir means to her—there's more in how Edvar spoke the name, and in Mara's refusal to explain it.
turns.summary: In Mara's garden, working the spring beds together, Mara names Silas Weir as a Harmonic stationed at the Heights and present at the contamination's edge—and reveals the true shape of her errand: find Silas, or report him to his own people.
turns.narration:
You lean on your spade and meet Mara's eyes directly. The rhythm of work gives you permission to ask what you've been holding back. "What does Silas Weir mean to you?" you say. "Edvar spoke his name like it breaks something. And you won't say who he is."

Mara doesn't stop turning the bed. Her spade meets the earth in steady time—push, turn, settle—and for a long moment you think she might not answer at all. Then her voice comes, even and careful, the way she speaks when the ledger matters.

"Silas is a Harmonic," she says. "Was stationed at the Heights before the readings got bad. He's good at what he does—reads the water's mood, knows what it wants to say. Or he was." She turns another section of soil. "Three weeks ago, Edvar saw him upstream at the contamination's edge. Silas was there with instruments—listening to something in the water that Edvar couldn't hear."

She pauses. The information sits between you like the spade between the beds.

"The choice I've been holding," Mara says finally, "is whether you go upstream to find him. Whether you carry what you've learned back to him, or whether you carry it to the Harmonic lodge and let them decide what to do with a man who might be at the center of this and might be the only one who understands it." Her eyes meet yours. "Either way, someone gets hurt. And I need to know you understand that before I ask it of you."

turns.player: Tell Mara you understand the weight—and that you'll need more information before you choose a path. Ask what she knows about where Silas was last seen.
turns.summary: In Mara's garden, Adelheid learns that Silas Weir—a Harmonic musician stationed at the Heights—was last seen upstream three weeks ago at the sluice-turn with tuning instruments, listening to something in the water. Since then, the river has worsened, suggesting a connection between what Silas heard and what is now poisoning the Echo.
turns.narration:
You set down your spade and meet Mara's eyes squarely, the garden beds around you still waiting for their turning. "I understand the weight of this," you say quietly. "But I need to know more before I choose. Where was Silas last seen? What were the instruments for?"

Mara's shoulders ease slightly—not relief, but something like recognition. She sets her own spade aside and picks up one of the cups from the bench, wrapping her hands around it. The steam rises between you both. "Upstream," she says. "Three weeks back, before the readings got worse. He was at the sluice-turn where the river broadens, the place where the current changes. Edvar saw him there with tuning equipment—the kind the Harmonics use to read what's underneath the noise."

She pauses, and you can see her working through what to say next—the calculation of a woman who measures her words like coin. "Edvar won't tell me what Silas was listening *for*. But he knows Silas heard something. Something that matters." Mara's eyes hold yours. "The water was clean then. Not pristine, but clean. Three weeks of degradation since he was at that sluice. That's not accident, Adelheid. That's sequence."

turns.player: Ask if Mara knows how to reach the sluice-turn, and whether the path is safe in spring melt.
turns.summary: In Mara Wells' garden, Adelheid asks how to reach the sluice-turn where Silas was last seen. Mara describes two routes: the direct path through the Wet Meadows (impassable until the spring melt subsides), or a longer climb through the terrace gardens and old stone-cuts. The choice crystallizes—wait, or take the longer way.
turns.narration:
You set your cup down on the bench, steam still rising from it, and ask the question that has been forming since Mara spoke Silas's name. "How do I reach the sluice-turn," you say. "And is the path safe in spring melt?"

Mara's expression settles into something practical—the look of someone who knows the land's moods and speaks them plainly. She gestures south and slightly east with one hand, the motion tracing the valley's slope. "The sluice-turn is upstream, where the current changes. You follow the Echo north from the mill for about two hours on foot—the bank is muddy but passable if you keep to the higher ground where the terrace roots hold the soil."

She pauses, turning her cup slowly in her hands. "The real trouble is the Wet Meadows. Spring melt floods them past the tree-line right now. Three weeks ago, when Silas went up there, the water was still manageable—but he would have gone through, not around." She looks at you directly. "If you mean to follow his path exactly, you'll wait another week or two until the melt subsides. If you mean to reach the sluice-turn another way, there's a higher route through the terrace gardens and into the old stone-cuts above the meadows. Takes longer, but the water won't stop you."

Aevi's motes brighten slightly at your shoulder, as if marking the two paths—the direct way Silas took, now impassable, and the longer climb that skirts the flood. The choice is plain now: move fast and wait, or move slow and reach.

history: [d2] You have found him waiting at the mill entrance. He is looking at you as though he has been expecting you, and has been waiting for you to arrive.

He refuses to accept you as Mara's simple messenger and insists you cannot hear what the water speaks—you came too…

[d2] He rejected your attempt at gentle silence. He spoke sharply: the river does not wait, and silence will not open him up. He has spent three weeks past the point where kindness helps. He demands direct engagement, not patience.

Edvar knows something about Silas that he has held close for three weeks

personalArc.name: The Root Remembers
personalArc.premise: A Swiss herbalist transplanted to an alien soil carries a silver-stemmed cutting from her village — the last living thread to everything she understood — and must decide whether her knowledge is a heritage to preserve or a seed to break open and replant entirely, in ground that does not know her name.
personalArc.stakes: To remain the keeper of a dead village's remedies, or to become something that village never imagined: a healer fluent in two earths, whose hands hold the old world and the new one at once — or to lose both trying.

legendNpc.name: The Silver-Stemmed Cutting
legendNpc.role: the last living root of her Swiss village, wrapped in linen and slowly dying, the mute accusation of every mile she was

stages.objective: the cutting that will not root — she has tried three times; the Korean soil rejects it, or she does not yet know how to ask; Mara Wells has seen this particular grief before, in other hands, and says so plainly

the remedy that should not work — she compounds a draught from Korean plants she only half-understands, borrowing Piotr's hard-won field notes, and it heals something her Swiss formulary swore was untreatable; the success feels like a betrayal, and a door

the linen unwrapped — the cutting is failing; she must choose what she owes it, what she owes Millbrook, and what she owes the healer she is becoming; the answer is in what she does with the roots when she finally opens the wrapping and faces what is left
